title: High-speed rail and what it is for

turns.speaker: Bronwen
turns.text: The northern leg's been cancelled, again, and the case was always sold on journey time. Twenty minutes saved.

turns.speaker: Teo
turns.text: Which was a terrible way to sell it. Nobody rearranges their life for twenty minutes.

turns.speaker: Iyla
turns.text: The real case is capacity. The line is full, and you can't run more freight or more local stopping services on a track that's already at its limit.

turns.speaker: Bronwen
turns.text: So building a fast line frees the old one for everything else.

turns.speaker: Iyla
turns.text: That's the whole point, and it's almost never the headline.

turns.speaker: Teo
turns.text: Because capacity doesn't photograph well and a fast train does.

turns.speaker: Bronwen
turns.text: The cost is genuinely hard to defend, mind you. Per mile, this is among the most expensive railway ever built anywhere.

turns.speaker: Iyla
turns.text: A lot of that is tunnelling to keep it out of sight of people who objected.

turns.speaker: Teo
turns.text: So the objections made it expensive, and the expense became the argument against it.

turns.speaker: Bronwen
turns.text: That circularity is real, though it isn't the whole story. The procurement was poor by any standard.

turns.speaker: Iyla
turns.text: There's also a serious question about which direction the benefit flows. Fast links to a capital can drain a smaller city rather than feed it.

turns.speaker: Teo
turns.text: Depends whether the smaller city has something the capital wants.

turns.speaker: Bronwen
turns.text: Which is not a question a railway can answer on its own.

points: A high-speed rail leg has been cancelled, having been justified mainly by journey time savings.
Teo argues time savings were a poor justification, as twenty minutes changes little.
Iyla identifies capacity as the real case, since a full line cannot carry more freight or local services.
Costs per mile are among the highest anywhere, partly due to tunnelling demanded by objectors, creating a circular argument.
Bronwen notes procurement was also poor by any standard.
Iyla raises the risk that fast links to a capital can drain smaller cities rather than strengthen them, which the railway alone cannot determine.
